title: An overview of the question–response system in American English conversation
abstract: Analyzes hundreds of questions from videotaped spontaneous American English conversations. It characterizes question types, social actions, and response types, providing empirical evidence about how natural responses satisfy or fail to fit prior questions.

admission.reason: The abstract gives useful empirical characterization of question and response types, but only at the question-response sequence level. It does not show question-to-span alignment, decomposition of multi-question messages, proposition-level answer scope, or identification of which subquestions remain unresolved. The more operational coding-scheme and multi-unit-question candidates admitted below strengthen the relevant streams more directly.

title: A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation
abstract: Develops and empirically motivates a model of turn-taking from naturally occurring conversation. Although it does not provide proposition-level computational annotations, its concepts of next-speaker selection, transition relevance, and recipient design are foundational for later empirical work on sequential response relations.

admission.reason: The work is foundational for conversational sequencing, but the supplied abstract does not provide proposition-level antecedent annotations, response-target identification, question-answer alignment, or scope judgments. Its turn-taking concepts are too indirect for the present reading round.

title: Getting at Discourse Referents
abstract: Uses conversational data to compare discourse-anaphoric uses of the pronoun it with demonstrative that. The empirical analysis examines how grammatical and attentional properties of earlier discourse determine which discourse referent is selected.
venue: 27th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The abstract establishes discourse-anaphoric reference in conversation but does not make clear whether the antecedents are specifically clauses, propositions, events, facts, or other non-nominal spans rather than ordinary discourse entities. Admission would require full-text evidence that the analysis explicitly identifies non-nominal antecedent spans or abstract discourse referents of the kind required by F1.

title: End-to-end dialogue structure parsing on multi-floor dialogue based on multi-task learning
abstract: Empirically studies dialogue structure in multi-floor collaborative robot-navigation conversations, where several concurrent conversational transactions may be active. The parser predicts antecedent links for utterances and then relation types, with dialogue-response prediction used as an auxiliary task.

admission.reason: The abstract clearly supports ordinary F2 antecedent-link and relation prediction, but it does not show partial reply scope, multiple antecedents, composite targets, ambiguity/no-link treatment, or multi-question answer resolution. Its core attachment capability is already represented more directly in this reading round by the VERIFIED structured dialogue parser 2306.15103, so this additional domain/model variant does not justify another slot.

title: Improving Multi-Party Dialogue Discourse Parsing via Domain Integration
abstract: Studies prediction of discourse dependency structure and relations between elementary discourse units in multi-party dialogue. It evaluates cross-domain attachment and relation prediction and develops domain-integration methods for transferring dialogue discourse parsers across conversational settings.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on Computational Approaches to Discourse

admission.reason: Although VERIFIED and clearly relevant to F2, the abstract is primarily about cross-domain improvement of ordinary discourse attachment and relation prediction. It does not add evidence for partial proposition scope, multi-antecedent responses, unanswered subquestions, or ambiguity/no-link behavior. For this gap-focused round, the F2 capability is sufficiently represented by the admitted VERIFIED structured parser 2306.15103.

title: Reformulation of questions with candidate answers
abstract: Studies a multi-unit format in which an open question is reformulated as a more specific yes-no question or a set of alternatives. The reformulation supplies candidate answers and changes the response space against which the recipient's subsequent answer is interpreted.

admission.reason: The abstract shows how reformulating an open question into a yes-no question or alternatives changes the recipient's response space, but it does not show annotation or prediction of which prior subquestion a response answers, whether only part is answered, or which parts remain unresolved. The phenomenon is relevant background but does not materially supply the target capability.

title: Coding Dialogs with the DAMSL Annotation Scheme
abstract: Describes the DAMSL dialogue-act annotation scheme and reports initial human-annotation reliability. Its backward communicative functions explicitly encode how a current utterance relates to earlier dialogue, including answering a question, accepting a proposal, and confirming understanding, while allowing multiple communicative functions on an utterance.
venue: Working Notes of the AAAI Fall Symposium on Communicative Action in Humans and Machines

admission.reason: DAMSL's backward communicative functions are relevant relation labels, including answer, acceptance, and confirmation, but the supplied abstract does not establish explicit proposition/span target pointers or scope boundaries. Multiple dialogue-act functions on one utterance are not evidence of multiple antecedents. For Topic 04 this is therefore primarily speech-act labeling without demonstrated antecedent scope, one of the stated false friends.

title: Non-Sentential Utterances in Dialogue: A: Corpus-Based Study
abstract: Presents a corpus-based study of non-sentential utterances in dialogue, including short answers and other fragments whose interpretation depends on prior conversational material. The analysis motivates explicit recovery of the contextual antecedent needed to interpret such responses.
venue: Proceedings of the Third SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

admission.reason: The abstract establishes that short and non-sentential responses require contextual antecedents, but it does not say whether the corpus explicitly annotates or evaluates antecedent selection, whether antecedents are proposition-level/non-nominal, or whether ambiguity and no-link cases are represented. Full text would need to show explicit antecedent representations or evaluated resolution relevant to F1 or F10.

title: A Deep Sequential Model for Discourse Parsing on Multi-Party Dialogues
abstract: Presents a sequential discourse parser for multi-party dialogue. For each elementary discourse unit, the model selects a previous EDU as its antecedent and predicts the corresponding discourse relation, jointly constructing a dialogue dependency structure.
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence

admission.reason: This VERIFIED paper directly implements F2 by selecting a previous EDU and predicting its discourse relation, but the abstract describes the standard single-antecedent dialogue-dependency problem and provides no evidence for partial response scope, multiple/composite antecedents, unresolved questions, or abstention. Its basic F2 contribution is duplicated in this reading round by the admitted VERIFIED structured parser 2306.15103.

title: Weak Supervision for Learning Discourse Structure
abstract: Evaluates weak-supervision strategies for learning discourse structure in multi-party dialogue. The experiments address discourse attachment rather than only relation classification, so the system must identify which earlier discourse unit a later contribution is linked to.
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing

admission.reason: The abstract concerns weak supervision for ordinary dialogue discourse attachment. It does not show the partial, ambiguous, multi-antecedent, no-link, or multi-question phenomena needed by the current gaps, and the underlying F2 attachment capability is already covered by an admitted VERIFIED paper.

title: A Structure Self-Aware Model for Discourse Parsing on Multi-Party Dialogues
abstract: Predicts discourse dependency structures for multi-party dialogues by modeling candidate EDU-to-EDU edges jointly rather than relying only on previous incremental decisions. Evaluation is performed on conversational discourse-parsing benchmarks where antecedent attachment and relation type must both be recovered.
venue: Proceedings of the Thirtieth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence

admission.reason: The joint edge-modeling approach materially concerns F2 discourse parsing, but the supplied abstract does not show multiple antecedents for one response, composite proposition targets, partial reply scope, or unanswered-question handling. It is another modeling variant for an already represented F2 capability rather than evidence that closes the current scope gaps.

title: Anaphora Resolution in Dialogue: Description of the DFKI-TalkingRobots System for the CODI-CRAC 2021 Shared-Task
abstract: Describes an anaphora-resolution system for dialogue whose discourse-deixis component detects discourse-anaphor and antecedent pairs. This component directly models links from referring expressions to prior discourse content rather than only entity coreference.
venue: Proceedings of the CODI-CRAC 2021 Shared Task on Anaphora, Bridging, and Discourse Deixis in Dialogue

admission.reason: The discourse-deixis component is directly relevant to F1, but this is a system description for a shared task. The admitted CODI-CRAC 2022 shared-task overview is more useful for this round because it exposes the conversational datasets, annotation task, and evaluation regime, while the admitted abstract-anaphora corpus provides complementary antecedent evidence. The supplied abstract does not show an additional scope or annotation capability that warrants another reading slot.

title: Scaling up from Dialogue to Multilogue: Some Principles and Benchmarks
abstract: Examines how dialogue interpretation mechanisms scale to conversations with more than two participants. Corpus evidence on non-sentential utterances is used to study contextual resolution, including cases where the relevant antecedent is not simply the immediately preceding contribution.
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The abstract indicates that non-sentential utterances in multilogue may resolve to non-adjacent contextual antecedents, which could strengthen F10. It does not establish whether antecedent candidates are explicitly annotated or evaluated, whether absent/ambiguous alternatives are preserved, or whether the antecedents are proposition-level. Full text would need to demonstrate one of those capabilities before admission.

title: Discourse Relation Prediction and Discourse Parsing in Dialogues with Minimal Supervision
abstract: Develops a semi-supervised pipeline that first predicts dialogue discourse structures and then discourse relations. Evaluation includes STAC and cross-domain technical chat, providing evidence about antecedent attachment in a conversational domain beyond game chat.
venue: Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Computational Approaches to Discourse (CODI 2024)

admission.reason: The abstract provides F2 attachment and relation prediction, including evaluation on technical chat, but it does not show partial response scope, multi-antecedent/composite targets, unresolved subquestions, or explicit no-link/ambiguity outcomes. Because the core F2 capability is already represented by VERIFIED 2306.15103, and this candidate is UNCHECKED, the verified paper is preferred for the reading slot.

title: Remarks on this and that
venue: Papers from the Tenth Regional Meeting of the Chicago Linguistic Society

admission.reason: No abstract was supplied. Admission requires evidence that the paper analyzes demonstratives whose antecedents are clauses, propositions, events, facts, situations, or other non-nominal discourse spans, rather than merely ordinary nominal demonstrative reference.

title: Some Facts About Centers, Indexicals, and Demonstratives
abstract: Empirically examines demonstrative and personal-pronoun reference in discourse. It shows that demonstratives can access discourse entities that are not the current local center, supporting antecedent-selection mechanisms that are not restricted to the immediately salient nominal referent.
venue: 29th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The abstract shows that demonstratives can select discourse entities outside the current local center, but it does not say whether those discourse entities are non-nominal propositions/events or ordinary nominal referents. Full text would need to establish abstract/propositional antecedent cases or an evaluated antecedent-selection scheme relevant to F1 or F10.
